connections.observation: The εὐδαίμων family recurs eleven times while ὅλος recurs six times with πόλις. The two families intersect at 420b-c and 420e-421c: Socrates insists the city is founded not so one group (ἕν τι ἔθνος) will be exceptionally happy but so the whole city (ὅλη ἡ πόλις) will be happy. The superlative εὐδαιμονέστατοί (420b) applied to guardians is subordinated to εὐδαιμονῇ (420e) governing ὅλη ἡ πόλις. This configuration makes visible a grammatical subordination of individual happiness claims to whole-city happiness claims, enacted through the verbal and adjectival choices themselves.

The dense cluster of possessions at 419a (fields, houses, furnishings, sacrifices, hospitality, gold and silver) is cited by Adeimantus as what guardians lack. χρυσός from this list reappears at 420e adorning farmers in Socrates' reductio. Held together, the two occurrences make visible a reversal: the possessions first named as marks of conventional happiness are then placed on craftsmen to show that such adornment destroys their function. The configuration turns the initial objection's evidence into the material of its own refutation.

The statue analogy at 420c-d introduces ἀνδριάντα γράφοντας and argues that eyes painted with purple (ὀστρείῳ) would ruin τὸ ὅλον καλόν. This figure is then explicitly mapped (καὶ δὴ καὶ νῦν, 420d) onto the city argument: do not compel us to attach happiness to guardians that makes them anything other than guardians. The analogy's τὸ ὅλον καλόν corresponds to ὅλη ἡ πόλις εὐδαιμονῇ (420e). The configuration makes visible that individual beauty (eyes) and individual happiness (one group) are treated through parallel grammatical and conceptual structures, both subordinated to a whole that they serve.

At 420e farmers are dressed in fine robes with gold, potters recline drinking; the parallel constructions articulate luxury incompatible with craft. At 420e-421a the doubled formulae (γεωργὸς γεωργός, κεραμεὺς κεραμεύς) state the result: each will no longer be what he is. The configuration makes visible a causal sequence: the parallel luxuries produce parallel destructions of identity, so that the doubling of the noun articulates a negation—the name remains but the thing named vanishes.

φύλαξ recurs six times; at 421a φύλακες νόμων τε καὶ πόλεως μὴ ὄντες ἀλλὰ δοκοῦντες appears. The being/seeming contrast also governs cobblers (νευρορράφοι προσποιησάμενοι εἶναι μὴ ὄντες, 421a). Held together with the repeated φύλαξ at 420e (ἢ φύλακας) and 421a (φύλακας ὡς ἀληθῶς), the configuration makes visible that guardians who merely seem to be guardians but are not destroy the city entirely (πᾶσαν ἄρδην πόλιν ἀπολλύασιν), while cobblers who seem but are not cause no harm (οὐδὲν δεινόν). The repetition of φύλαξ around the being/seeming distinction articulates asymmetry in consequence.

πλοῦτος and πενία are named together at 421d and repeated at 422a. At 422a each is assigned a triad of vices: wealth produces τρυφή, ἀργία, νεωτερισμός; poverty produces ἀνελευθερία, κακοεργία, and also νεωτερισμός. The configuration makes visible that the paired opposites share one result (νεωτερισμός) while differing in their other effects. The section's closing sentence thus preserves a double asymmetry: wealth and poverty are opposites that converge on one shared corruption while diverging in others.

ἐπίκουροι appears first at 419a-420a in Adeimantus's objection (hired mercenaries who merely guard) and returns at 421b-c where Socrates groups ἐπικούρους with φύλακας, requiring both to be ἄριστοι δημιουργοὶ τοῦ ἑαυτῶν ἔργου. The configuration makes visible that the word initially cited as a negative comparison is retained and assigned positive function: auxiliaries are craftsmen of their own work, not mere hirelings. The recurrence transforms the term's role from objection to solution.

βλέπω recurs three times articulating direction of attention. At 420b οὐ πρὸς τοῦτο βλέποντες denies founding the city for one group's exceptional happiness. At 421b the verb appears twice: πρὸς τοῖτο βλέποντες τοὺς φύλακας καθιστῶμεν poses looking toward guardians' maximal happiness, while εἰς τὴν πόλιν ὅλην βλέποντας θεατέον counters with looking toward the whole city. The threefold recurrence makes visible a spatial grammar of attention in which πρὸς τοῦτο and εἰς τὴν πόλιν ὅλην are opposed directions, and the correct direction must be discerned (θεατέον) rather than assumed.

μακάριος appears at 419a describing those conventionally expected to be blessed (τοῖς μέλλουσιν μακαρίοις εἶναι) and at 420e in the reductio making all craftsmen μακαρίους. The parallel luxuries assigned to farmers and potters at 420e (fine robes, gold, reclining, feasting) realize what μακάριος conventionally signifies. Held together, the two occurrences make visible that the objection's own standard of blessedness—the μακάριοι who possess fields, houses, gold—is shown to destroy craft identity when enacted. The term moves from naming a conventional expectation to naming an impossible condition.

ἀπολογέομαι appears three times: Adeimantus challenges Socrates to defend (ἀπολογήσῃ, 419a), Socrates takes up the defense (ἀπολογησόμεθα, 420b), and the statue analogy models a measured defense (μετρίως ἂν ἐδοκοῦμεν ἀπολογεῖσθαι, 420d). The third occurrence introduces the hypothetical critic (προσελθών τις ἔψεγε) and the imagined reply. The sequence makes visible that the actual defense is performed through analogy: the statue-painter's reply to a hypothetical objection becomes the form of Socrates' reply to Adeimantus's actual objection, so that ἀπολογεῖσθαι enacted in one domain is transferred to govern the other.

δημιουργός appears three times. At 421c guardians and auxiliaries are to be ἄριστοι δημιουργοὶ τοῦ ἑαυτῶν ἔργου. At 421d-e the argument turns to how other δημιουργοί are corrupted. At 421e a corrupted craftsman produces χείρους δημιουργούς through teaching. At 420e-421a the doubled formulae (γεωργὸς γεωργός, κεραμεὺς κεραμεύς) state loss of identity. Held together, the configuration makes visible that δημιουργός names both guardians and other craftsmen: guardians must be craftsmen of their own work, while other craftsmen who gain wealth or suffer poverty cease to be craftsmen and produce inferior craftsmen. The term articulates a shared standard (excellence in one's ἔργον) whose loss or retention determines whether the nominal identity persists.

The εὐδαίμων family saturates the section's first two-thirds, culminating at 421c with εὐδαιμονίας as the goal distributed by nature to each group. At 422a the section closes with the vices produced by πλοῦτος (τρυφή, ἀργία, νεωτερισμός) and πενία (ἀνελευθερία, κακοεργία, νεωτερισμός). No form of εὐδαίμων appears in the closing passage. The configuration makes visible a substitution: the question of happiness, repeated eleven times, is resolved into the question of wealth and poverty's corruption. The answer to the challenge about guardians' εὐδαιμονία arrives as the naming of what must be guarded against, not as a positive account of εὐδαιμονία itself.

φύλαξ recurs six times; at 421e φυλακτέον appears: ἃ παντὶ τρόπῳ φυλακτέον ὅπως μήποτε αὐτοὺς λήσει εἰς τὴν πόλιν παραδύντα. The question τὰ ποῖα ταῦτα; is answered with πλοῦτός τε καὶ πενία. The configuration makes visible that φύλαξ (guardian) and φυλακτέον (must be guarded against) share a root, so the guardians must guard against the very things (wealth and poverty) that would destroy their function as guardians. The etymological relation articulates a reflexive structure: guardians guard against what would make them not-guardians.

elements.context: ὅπως ὅτι ἄριστοι δημιουργοὶ τοῦ ἑαυτῶν ἔργου ἔσονται
χείρω μὲν τὰ τῶν τεχνῶν ἔργα

new_signals.observation: ἔργον (work, product) recurs three times: guardians are to be best craftsmen of their own ἔργον (421c), then wealth/poverty cause inferior ἔργα to be produced (421e, twice). The recurrence links guardians' work to craftsmen's products under a shared term.

elements.context: τοῦ μὲν τρυφὴν καὶ ἀργίαν καὶ νεωτερισμὸν ἐμποιοῦντος
τῆς δὲ ἀνελευθερίαν καὶ κακοεργίαν πρὸς τῷ νεωτερισμῷ

new_signals.observation: νεωτερισμός appears twice in the final sentence, once as the third vice produced by wealth and once as the final element (πρὸς τῷ) added to poverty's vices. The repeated word closes both halves of the paired structure.

elements.context: ὅπως μήποτε αὐτοὺς λήσει εἰς τὴν πόλιν παραδύντα

new_signals.observation: παραδύντα (sneaking in, slipping in) describes how πλοῦτος and πενία might enter the city unnoticed (λήσει). The verb articulates covert entry rather than open arrival.

elements.context: χείρω μὲν τὰ τῶν τεχνῶν ἔργα

new_signals.observation: τέχνη appears three times in the wealth/poverty argument (421d-e): a wealthy potter will not care for his craft, poverty prevents acquiring tools for the craft, and both corrupt the products of the crafts.
